content.title: Author response to Reviewer L47e
content.comment:
>*Q1:* Although metrics like ROUGE are commonly used for evaluating summarization tasks, high score text might not be very fluent/coherent, especially when generators are trained by RL objective optimizing for ROUGE/BLEU. 
  
A1: We appreciate your valuable advice. Due to more than 90% of papers only reporting ROUGE scores on summarization tasks, we follow these works. And we totally agree with you that adding the human judge metric will be better, and we will add these results in our final version (due to time limitation, we cannot add it in the rebuttal).  To compensate, we use FactCC (Kryscinski et al. (2019), [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.12840.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.12840.pdf)) and QuestEval (Scialom et al. (2021), [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12693.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12693.pdf)) to measure the faithfulness of the model. These metrics use a trained language model to assess the factual consistency between the generated summary and the input source document. We also use BERTScore (Zhang et al. (2020), [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09675.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09675.pdf)), which measures the semantic similarity of the predicted summary and the reference summary. The table below shows the performance of BART and JGR on these three advanced metrics on CNN/DM: 
  
|         | BERTScore | FactCC   |QE    | 
|----------|---------|---------|---------| 
|BART     |88.47    |57.54    |  59.41    | 
| JGR-G    |88.90   |60.33    | 61.53   | 
| JGR-R    |88.96   |61.59    |   61.62      | 
  
As shown in the table, JGR-G and JGR-R both achieve higher BERTScore than BART, indicating that they can generate summaries with better semantic quality. For FactCC and QuestEval, which measures factual consistency, JGR-G and JGR-R also surpass the BART baseline. These results demonstrate that JGR, despite optimizing for ROUGE, does not compromise on other aspects of summary quality, such as semantic similarity and factual consistency, and can even improve on them compared to the generator trained with NLL. We add the above results to Appendix C in the rebuttal revision.  
  
Moreover, JGR is not limited to ROUGE and BLEU as the ranking criteria. It could potentially perform better if we incorporate other metrics like FactCC into $\Delta(\mathbf{\hat{y}}, \mathbf{y})$. We plan to add these results to the appendix of the revision and explore this direction in the future. 
  
Hope our reply has solved your concerns, if you have any other questions please feel free to let us know, we will try our best to answer for you.

content.title: Author response: the human evaluation results
content.comment:
We have completed the human evaluation on CNN/DailyMail. Following Blenderbot v2 (Roller et al., 2020 [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.13637.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.13637.pdf)), we ask the annotators to explicitly compare which generated text is better for each pair of generated outputs, rather than assign an evaluation score. This explicit comparison can avoid the per annotator bias in numerical scores (e.g., annotators who tend to give generous scores), and remedy many of the issues of sequential effects such as contrasting with a previous case. We randomly picked 100 cases from the CNN/DailyMail test set, each case was organized as `<Doc, Summary #1, Summary #2>` where `Doc` means the source document, `Summary #1` and `Summary #2` mean the summaries generated by JGR and BART. 

The annotators were asked to compare `Summary #1` and `Summary #2` on three aspects given at the end of each case. To avoid the stereotype of annotators that `Summary #1` or `Summary #2` is better according to previous cases, we randomly shuffle the summaries in each case, which means that `Summary #1` is not necessarily from JGR or BART, and so as `Summary #2`.

Each picked case was annotated by 3 annotators, and they worked individually without communication. Given a certain human evaluation metric on one case, the comparison result is obtained by the following rules:

1. If more than or equal to two annotators think JGR has won in that metric, then JGR wins.
2. If more than or equal to two annotators think BART has won in that metric, then BART wins.
3. Otherwise, the comparison result is marked as a tie.

We evaluate JGR and BART from three aspects, namely informativeness (Inform.), factual consistency (Fact.), and readability (Read.). The results are shown below:


|  | JGR wins| Tie| JGR loses|
|---|-------|-----|-----|
|Inform.|58|3|39|
|Fact. |61|7|32|
|Read. |45|15|40|


As shown in the results, JGR beats BART in 58 cases w.r.t informativeness and 61 cases w.r.t. factual consistency, indicating that JGR performs better than BART on informativeness and factual consistency. For readability, JGR can generate summaries as readable as BART. To conclude, though trained with reinforcement learning aimed at optimizing ROUGE score, JGR still outperforms BART w.r.t. informativeness and factual consistency, and the readability is not harmed. Note that since we use direct comparison, the number of “tie” cases may be fewer than some works that conduct human evaluation through assigning scores. We also release the detail of human evaluation together with the annotation results of the 3 annotators in our opensource link ([https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597]( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597)).

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper deals with the two-stage generation -> rerank framework in text generation. The authors train a model that integrates the generator and the ranker. The approach is called JGR. JGR is trained with a contrastive loss that compares the generator outputs. Experiments are done on CNN/DailyMail summarization, SAMSum, SQuAD v1.1, PersonaChat. JGR obtains good results, including state-of-the-art results on CNN/DM in terms of ROUGE-1/2/L. Using BRIO (bridging order to abstractive summarization by Liu et al.) initialization for summarization further improves the ROUGE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Integrating generation and ranking is an important problem and deserves more attention. The authors’ intention of using contrastive learning is great. 

The discussion in Section 4.6 and Section 4.7 (whether joint training matters) is inspiring. 

Experiments are done on multiple tasks including summarization, question answering (SQuAD), and dialogue (PersonaChat).  

Some of the missing references
- Zhong et al. (2020), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.08795.pdf: essentially contrastive-learning-based reranking (also search work related to Zhong et al. / Zhong et al. cited / cites Zhong et al.)
- Liu et al. (2021), return-based contrastive representation learning for RL: https://openreview.net/forum?id=_TM6rT7tXke 
- Contrastive learning for ranking in summarization (inspired by Zhong et al. above):  https://aclanthology.org/2022.coling-1.508.pdf 
- RL for integrating generation+ranking in machine translation for related work in Section 2.1: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.08670.pdf 
There are papers that proposed contrastive learning for reranking, but are missing in this paper. I’m fine with this paper’s approach, but an explanation of the pros and cons of the authors’ approach with respect to the previous papers is needed imo. 

The approach is very similar to RL. In RL, models are optimized toward higher-ranked generations. In this work, D is optimized so that it can differentiate higher-ranked generations and lower-ranked generations. The difference between this work and RL (and why this work is better than RL) can be explained further. More importantly, RL baselines are important and should be described and experimented in more detail. For example, REINFORCE/PPO using well-designed baselines (the baseline that is subtracted from rewards) should be baselines and they should be well-tuned. But they are currently missing from the tables. Please correct me if I’m missing anything obvious.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think people usually refer to CNN/DailyMail as extractive summarization instead of abstractive summarization (as in Section 4.1). 

Averaging ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L doesn’t make sense to me at least personally.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Using contrastive learning to make sure the ranker ranks higher-scored generations, to integrate the generation-ranking problem, is important. Discussion with some related work is missing. Experimental results are quite encouraging. I'm not confident if RL baselines are strong enough.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer nPC9 (part-1)
content.comment:
>*Q1:* There are papers that proposed contrastive learning for reranking, but are missing in this paper.  
 
A1: We appreciate your reminder and will cite the papers you mentioned. We would love to describe the difference between JGR and these works.  
 
The main difference between the 1st, 3rd, and 4th papers and our JGR is that our goal is not to compress the generate-then-rank pipeline into a single model, but to jointly train the generator and ranker. Our empirical results in Section 4.5 and Section 4.7 show that a joint-trained ranker benefits the training of generator. In contrast, the 1st, 3rd, and 4th papers propose to compress generate-then-rank pipeline into a single model and use a fixed function (evaluation metrics or fixed models) to rank the candidates, without the benefit of a co-trained ranker. For the 2nd paper (Liu et al. (2021)), it is not very relevant to our work, as it applies contrastive learning to enhance the representative ability of state-action encoder in RL models for Atari games, while our work focuses on NLG, and contrastive learning is used to train the ranker in JGR.   
 

 
>*Q2:* The difference between this work and RL (and why this work is better than RL) can be explained further.   
 
A2: Thanks for the suggestion, we hope that we’ve addressed the misunderstanding in the new version of the paper. We would like to clarify that JGR doesn’t propose a new training paradigm different from RL, but it follows the RL framework, especially for generator model training. 
 
However, different from conventional RL based language generation approaches which adopt i.e., BLEU/Rouge scores as the rewards, JGR uses the jointly trained ranker to assign contrastive rewards to each generation candidate which has shown substantial improvement over generation quality. Overall, the advantages of JGR over conventional RL can be summarized as follows:  
 
1. Ranker could provide more diverse positive and negative reward signals to generation candidates than static BLEU/Rouge based rewards. 
 
2. The iterative joint training of the ranker-generator model can further lift the generation performance by allowing ranker and generator to learn from each other, which is inspired from GAN-based training paradigm.   
 
>*Q3:* RL baselines are important and should be described and experimented in more detail.  For example, REINFORCE/PPO using well-designed baselines (the baseline that is subtracted from rewards) should be baselines and they should be well-tuned. 
 
A3: Thanks for the comments. We will make it clearer in the paper about the baseline setup. The RL baseline we used in the experiment is called the self-critic approach, which uses the metric score of the greedy search generation as the baseline following the work of Rennie et al. (2017) and Paulus et al. (2018) that we cited in Section 4.5.  
 
We also add the results of a simple actor-critic method in the revised version of the rebuttal. The critic is trained to fit the output score of a sampled candidate to the evaluation metric score, and it feeds back the output score to the generator (actor) as the reward. The results are shown below (we add this result to Appendix A.1 in the rebuttal revision):  

|          | R-1     | R-2     |R-L     | AVG    |  
|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------|  
| RL       | 44.14  |21.20    |40.95    |   35.43|   
|actor-critic|45.04    |21.99    |41.71    |36.25    |  
| JGR-G   |46.86     |23.18    |43.74   |37.93    |  



In the current version of our paper, we implemented the self-critic RL method and actor-critic method following (Rennie et al. (2017) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf), Le et al. (2022) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf)) and took them as the RL-based compared methods. We totally agree with you that PPO can be added as a baseline and we will add the performance of PPO in the next version.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer nPC9 (part-2)
content.comment:
> *Q4:* I think people usually refer to CNN/DailyMail as extractive summarization instead of abstractive summarization (as in Section 4.1)  

A4: We appreciate your reminder and, following Newsroom (Grusky et al. (2018), [https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11283]( https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11283) ), we calculated the extractive fragment coverage (EFC) and extract fragment density (EFD) of CNN/DM and SAMSum: 

| Dataset  | EFC  | EFD  |
|----------|---------|---------|
| CNN/DM | 0.8|   3|   
|SAMSum| 0.4 | 0.8 |  


The results indicate that CNN/DM has high EFC and EFD, meaning that it is more “extractive”. We will revise the description of CNN/DM in section 4.1 accordingly in the revision. On the other hand, many recent works have tackled the CNN/DM task in an abstractive way. Our results also demonstrate that JGR can perform well on both relatively “extractive” datasets (CNN/DM) and relatively “abstractive” datasets (SAMSum).  


>*Q5:* Averaging ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L doesn’t make sense to me at least personally.  

A5: Thanks for the suggestion. Averaging ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L as the overall score of ROUGE just for quantization of the overall generation performance.  Some leaderboards, such as GLUE, will average the different metric scores on different datasets to show an overall score of models.  However, we do not take this average as an important basis to judge the performance of models. All the figures we showed in the paper exclude the average ROUGE score, and all the conclusions about the summarization models in this paper are drawn according to ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L. 


Hope our reply has solved your concerns, if you have any other questions, please feel free to let us know, we will try our best to answer for you.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper propose a joint training framework for learning a generator and a ranker simultaneously. Multiple training objectives are combined (contrastive, maximum likelihood, and reinforcement learning) to train the models. The experiments are thoroughly conducted. content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

**Simple and clear method**: the method proposed by this paper (train the ranker with contrastive learning and train of generator with NLL and RL) is simple, clear, and intuitive.

**Overall effectiveness**: this paper does a good work in establishing clear comparisons in the experiments, showing a clear performance gain over clearly comparable baselines (e.g., in Table 2, JGR init w. BRIO outperforms BRIO by a clear margin)

**Extensive experiments**: in addition to the overall performance gain, the authors further provide interesting and extensive studies on more detailed aspects like ranker performance, rewards, and candidate picking strategies, which further make the experiments stronger. 

**Weakness** 

**Novelty**: all techniques used in this paper (joint training, contrastive training, RL+NLL training) are already discussed in various previous papers. This paper is more like an ensemble of these existing techniques that are empirically effective. Although combining and applying existing techniques to new scenarios is a solid contribution on itself, this paper lacks the intellectual originality especially for a venue like ICLR.

**One additional suggestion**: it would be good if there is a navigating paragraph at the beginning of the experiments telling the readers about how and why the experiments are organized this way. The currently writing directly jumps to the experimental details and the readers have to take efforts to figure out the relationship between the experiments, which is prone to misunderstanding or not understanding well enough.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality of this paper is high: simple and clear method and solid experiments. The novelty of this paper is not very high, as most of the technique are proposed by existing works. This work should not be hard to reproduce if codes are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am ambiguous about this work. On the one hand, this paper is clearly motivated, the method is intuitive and effective. The experimental results are strong, solid, and extensive. On the other hand, this paper is a combination of existing techniques (which on itself is also of research value) yet lacks intellectual originality. Combining these considerations, I would rate this paper as marginal acceptance.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer xGN5
content.comment:
>*Q1:* All techniques used in this paper (joint training, contrastive training, RL+NLL training) are already discussed in various previous papers. This paper is more like an ensemble of these existing techniques that are empirically effective. 

A1: Thank you for acknowledging our contribution. Several works in NLG, especially the GAN/RL-based methods (Rennie et al. (2017) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf); Le et al. (2022) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf); Yu et al. (2017) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf)), adopt the joint training and RL techniques. While our JGR stills make some improvements upon these works. Different from conventional RL-based language generation approaches which adopt i.e., BLEU/Rouge scores as the rewards, JGR uses the ranker model to assign contrastive rewards to each generation candidate which has shown substantial improvement over generation quality (in Figure 2) and diversity (in Figure 4) in our experiment. 

Compared with generator-discriminator approaches based (i.e., GAN), JGR doesn’t seek to optimize an overall mini-max objective function, which allows more flexibility in terms of reward design, i.e., the comparison with different reward functions in Table 5 and Figure 2 and the comparison with different ranker model in Table 4 show that we can significantly improve the performance of pre-trained language models by training the ranker model with proper reward design.
 
On the other hand, for the basic techniques used in JGR, we also make some improvements:  
  
1.    We design a different objective for the ranker in JGR than for the discriminators. The ranker does not learn to tell apart the ground truth reference and the candidates, but to rank, the candidates sampled from the generator. This way, the ranker can concentrate on
ranking the candidates, without being misled by the ground truth reference during training. This improves the performance of the generate-then-rank pipeline and provides more accurate rewards for the generator.  
  
2.  The traditional reinforcement learning-based NLG methods, such as value-based RL and actor-critic, sample one single output per training step. Different from them, we train the generator to sample several i.i.d. candidates at each training step, and assign their rewards by the ranker contrastively. It allows the generator to be optimized on a more diverse probability of candidates and to reward the good candidates while penalizing the bad candidates. Our empirical results in Section 4.6 show the contribution of sampling several candidates. We add an experiment in Appendix A.1 in the rebuttal revision, demonstrating the performance superiority of JGR compared with reinforcement learning methods (value-based RL and Actor-critic). The results are as the table shown below: 
  
|          | R-1     | R-2     |R-L     | AVG    | 
|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------| 
| RL       | 44.14  |21.20    |40.95    |   35.43|  
|actor-critic|45.04    |21.99    |41.71    |36.25    | 
| JGR-G   |46.86     |23.18    |43.74   |37.93    | 
  
  
>*Q2:* It would be good if there is a navigating paragraph at the beginning of the experiments telling the readers about how and why the experiments are organized this way. 
  
A2: Thank you for your advice, we added a navigating paragraph in the revised edition of this paper. 
  
Hope our reply has solved your concerns, if you have any other questions
please feel free to let us know, we will try our best to answer for you.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer cvjv
content.comment:
> *Q1:* The joint training of a generator and a reward function generator is not new. The paper basically replaced the discriminator score in the existing work with the reranking score. 
  
A1：We appreciate your advice to help us improve this paper. We have detailed discussion of the connection between JGR and GAN/Actor-Critic in Appendix A.1 and A.2. To be brief, the proposed JGR follows the reinforcement learning framework for language generation. However, different with conventional RL based language generation approaches which adopts i.e., BLEU/Rouge scores as the rewards, JGR uses the ranker model to assign contrastive rewards to each generation candidate which has shown substantial improvement over generation quality (in Figure 2) and diversity (in Figure 4) in our experiment.  Compared with generator-discriminator approaches based (i.e., GAN), JGR doesn’t seek optimizing an overall mini-max objective function, which allows more flexibility in terms of reward design, i.e., the comparison with different reward functions in Table 5 and Figure 2 and the comparison with different ranker model in Table 4 show that we can significantly improve the performance of pretrained language models by training the ranker model with proper reward design. 
 
We understand that you suggest moving them to the main section of the paper. We are grateful for your recognition, and we will do so in the next version of this paper.  
 
 
> *Q2:* The use of BLEU score to measure diversity in sec 4.7 although reasonable but may not be well correlated. The author should consider more appropriate metrics such as Distinct n-gram or entropy to measure if joint training actually generates more diverse outputs or not. 
 
 
A2: To measure the diversity of candidates sampled for a single input source, we use self-BLEU instead of the corpus-level diversity of the outputs. As introduced in Appendix B, the self-BLEU score is the average BLEU score of each pair of candidates in the sampled set. A higher self-BLEU score indicates a higher similarity between the candidates, and thus a lower sequence-level diversity for a single input. Another way to assess the diversity of sampled candidates is to use Distinct n-gram, which calculates the ratio of distinct n-grams to the total number of tokens for the sampled candidates of an input sequence. A higher Distinct n-gram value implies a higher diversity of sampled candidates. We define self-Distinct-n as the Distinct n-gram for the sampled candidates of a single input. We plot the changes of self-Distinct-2 for JGR and JGR$_{\text{w/o joint}}$ during training: 
  
|          | 500| 1500|2500 | 3500 | 4500| 5500 | 6500 | 
|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------| 
|JGR| 45.30| 50.32 | 51.29 | 47.25 | 52.76 | 47.06 | 54.63| 
|JGR$_{\text{w/o joint}}$ |44.92|  43.59 |31.38| 26.39 | 25.59 |27.30 |27.49 | 
  
We observe that the self-Distinct-2 of JGR$_{\text{w/o joint}}$ drops sharply after 1000 steps of generator training, while the self-Distinct-2 of JGR remains relatively high throughout the training. This phenomenon is consistent with what we found using self-BLEU. Similar to Figure 4 in the paper, we present the curves of the average self-Distinct-2 for generated candidates at each training interval in Figure 5 in the revised version of this paper. 
  
Hope our reply has solved your concerns, if you have any other questions please feel free to let us know, we will try our best to answer for you.

replying_to: Replying to Joint Generator-Ranker Learning for Natural Language Generation

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewers’ insightful and constructive feedback. We have provided a separate response to each reviewer and also updated the paper following the revision suggestions of the reviewers. The main revision content is as follows:

1. We add more details about the compared self-critic RL method we compared in Section 4.5. We detailly introduce the reward and baseline used in the self-critic RL method.
2. Apart from the self-BLEU, we add the self-Distinct metric to measure the diversity of generated candidates. We show the curves of the average self-Distinct-2 for generated candidates at each training interval in Figure 5. And the results are consistent with what we found when applying self-BLEU, enhancing the conclusion in Section 4.7 that with joint training, the generator can keep a certain level of diversity in sampled candidates.
3. We compare related works mentioned by Reviewer Npc9 with our JGR in Section 2.2.
4. We implement a new RL method, i.e. the actor-critic method Le et al. (2022) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf). And compare it with our JGR on CNN/DailyMail, as a comparison between JGR and traditional RL methods that jointly train a critic model. The results are in Table 9.
5. We use three new advanced metrics, i.e. BERTScore, FactCC, and QuestEval, to evaluate JGR on CNN/DailyMail. The results are in Table 12, which indicate that despite JGR being optimized for evaluation metrics like ROUGE, it does not compromise on other aspects of summary quality, such as semantic similarity and factual consistency, and can even improve on them compared to the generator trained with NLL.

The baseline approaches in the paper, including self-critic reinforcement learning approach (referred to as “RL” in the paper), actor-critic, and GAN are implemented by following the works Rennie et al. (2017) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00563.pdf), Le et al. (2022) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf]( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf) and Yu et al. (2017) [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01780.pdf), respectively. We use the same model selection strategy for all baselines and proposed JGR approach: It selects the model which achieves the best performance on validation set. The source code and pre-trained model checkpoints (including RL, AC, GAN, JGR) are released at the following anonymous github link currently:  [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597) and the official github link would be released soon after the anonymous paper-review period. 

If there are any other questions that we did not address in the response, please feel free to let us know and we would be happy to provide further explanation.

content.title: Human evaluation results are provided
content.comment: We have conducted human evaluation comparing JGR and BART on CNN/DailyMail. The results show that though trained with reinforcement learning aimed at optimizing ROUGE score, JGR still outperforms BART w.r.t. informativeness and factual consistency, and the readability is not harmed. For more details, please refer to our response to Reviewer L47e ([https://openreview.net/forum?id=94WEPuo8D_a&noteId=ur0t_dm4zsh](https://openreview.net/forum?id=94WEPuo8D_a&noteId=ur0t_dm4zsh)). We also release the detail of human evaluation together with the annotation results of the 3 annotators in our opensource link ([https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597]( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jgr-anonymous-F597)).
